topic: psychological attributes and household inflation expectations
selection_note: Ten substantive sources prioritize direct household inflation-expectation measures, experiments, panel or administrative linkage, and explicit contrary evidence; an official GSS codebook record documents item measurement. No public full texts were downloaded locally. Reading status states whether full text, selected sections, or abstract only was reviewed.

sources.title: General Social Survey 2024 Codebook
authors: NORC at the University of Chicago
sources.access_level: Official codebook entries for HAPPY, SATFIN and GOODLIFE reviewed; not a microdata analysis.

evidence_locations.claim: General happiness asks whether the respondent is very happy, pretty happy, or not too happy; the response scale is ordinal.
Financial satisfaction asks whether the respondent is pretty well satisfied, more or less satisfied, or not satisfied at all; the response scale is ordinal.
GOODLIFE is an ordered agreement item about whether the respondent and family have a good chance of improving their standard of living. It is not an inflation forecast.

findings: The named GSS measures are ordered answer categories, not continuous, precisely measured psychological scores.
GOODLIFE is one possible economic-prospect measure, but the codebook alone does not establish that ConsumerSim used this item for its 'future optimism' attribute.
limitations: The 2024 codebook documents item wording and response categories; it does not establish availability in every GSS year or the exact source version, coding and conditional cells used by ConsumerSim.
Item documentation is not evidence that happiness or satisfaction causes inflation expectations.
sources.project_use: Preserve ordinal categories and item wording if these constructs are later examined. Do not infer a paper's specific variable mapping from similar construct names.

sources.title: Uncovering Salience-Driven Dynamics in Consumer Confidence with Generative Social Simulation
sources.access_level: Full HTML read for §§2.5, 4.2.1–4.2.2 and relevant implementation text.

evidence_locations.claim: Lists happiness, financial satisfaction, job satisfaction, future optimism, social trust and perceived mobility as attributes statistically imputed from conditional GSS distributions; says they are not direct measures of particular SIPP individuals.
The persona ablation removes the entire Hierarchical Persona Substrate, not one psychological attribute at a time.

findings: The paper names the behavioral attributes and their GSS-based conditional-imputation approach.

The reported ablation shows a contribution from the overall persona substrate, including demographics and household circumstances, but does not identify the incremental value of any one psychological attribute.
limitations: The paper does not provide in §4.2 item names, conditioning cells, pooled-year details, or uncertainty for each imputed psychological attribute.
The target is consumer confidence, not SCE one-year inflation expectations or Q9 subjective densities.
sources.project_use: Use only as a framework precedent. Do not cite it as evidence that happiness or optimism individually improves SCE expectation simulation.

sources.title: Expectations of Inflation: The Role of Demographic Variables, Expectation Formation, and Financial Literacy
sources.access_level: Full article HTML read; sample, measures, tables and discussion checked.

evidence_locations.claim: RAND American Life Panel module; lower objective financial literacy and greater attention to paying future expenses / prices paid are associated with higher one-year inflation expectations.

Self-reported focus on the U.S. inflation rate and subjective financial confidence are not significantly related to reported expectations; lower financial literacy groups show greater expectation disagreement.

findings: This is direct household inflation-expectation evidence linking financial attention and objective financial literacy to forecast levels.
It distinguishes actual knowledge from confidence in one's knowledge; the latter was not a significant predictor in the reported models.
limitations: Observational correlations in a module of 299 panel members, not a randomized numeracy treatment.
The sample was recruited through Michigan survey respondents, skewed toward higher education and income, and the survey dates to 2007–2008.
The study measures point expectations and does not establish how these attributes affect SCE Q9 probability densities.
sources.project_use: Prioritize verified numeracy/financial-understanding measures over a generic confidence or satisfaction score; test response format and subgroup fit separately.

sources.title: Inflation Expectations and Behavior: Do Survey Respondents Act on Their Beliefs?
sources.source_type: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Staff Report 509
sources.access_level: Abstract, introduction, sample, measures and results in §§1–2 read in the 51-page PDF; not every section reread.

evidence_locations.claim: Survey inflation beliefs are compared with choices in a financially incentivized investment experiment; respondents whose choices are difficult to rationalize score lower on numeracy and financial literacy and take longer to complete the survey.

findings: Survey inflation beliefs correlate with decisions whose payoffs depend on future inflation, supporting a degree of construct validity.
Numeracy and financial literacy may affect how respondents convert beliefs into probability and financial choices.
limitations: The experiment validates a narrow financial choice, not every real-world action or the accuracy of an inflation forecast.
The 2010–2011 U.S. American Life Panel sample was recruited from Michigan survey participants and is not the current SCE panel.
sources.project_use: Use as evidence about probability comprehension and response behavior, not as proof that higher numerical ability makes expectations more accurate.

sources.title: Trust in the Central Bank and Inflation Expectation
sources.access_level: Full 47-page PDF read; survey design, regressions, IV discussion and appendix checked.

evidence_locations.claim: 2015 Dutch CentERpanel survey, 3,117 observations; higher ECB trust is associated with lower average one-year expectation and individual uncertainty, with a stronger anchoring pattern in the upper forecast quantiles.
The paper controls for ECB knowledge, financial literacy and optimism; IV uses repair-person cheating exposure and interpersonal trust under explicit exclusion assumptions.

findings: Trust can relate to both the level and the respondent's own uncertainty; the level association is not uniform across the distribution.
Trust and expected GDP growth move positively together in this setting, underscoring that expected output and expected inflation are separate outcomes.
limitations: The design is an observational panel survey with IV assumptions, not randomized assignment of trust.
The result concerns Dutch-speaking households, ECB credibility and a 2015 low-inflation setting, not U.S. SCE 2021 one-year Q9.
sources.project_use: Treat trust as a possible anchor and moderator, not a fixed coefficient that uniformly lowers every simulated household's forecast. Keep within-person uncertainty distinct from between-person disagreement.

sources.title: Would Households Understand Average Inflation Targeting?
sources.source_type: Journal of Monetary Economics article; Bundesbank Discussion Paper 17/2022 author version
sources.access_level: Full 50-page Bundesbank PDF read; design, abstract, main results and appendix checked.

evidence_locations.claim: About 9,000 Bundesbank Online Panel Households respondents took part in randomized information treatments about a hypothetical average-inflation-targeting regime; high trust strengthened policy-consistent updates, while the lowest-trust group could revise in the opposite direction.

findings: Trust changes how a household responds to a specific policy-information treatment; it does not imply a universal sign for expected inflation.
The experiments elicit probabilistic medium- and longer-term expectations, so they distinguish information response from stable optimism.
limitations: The policy regime was hypothetical and the setting was Germany/ECB; the horizon is two to three or five to ten years, not SCE's one year.
Trust itself was measured rather than randomized, although the information treatment was randomized.
sources.project_use: A strong design precedent for testing trust × message interactions; do not translate its treatment effect directly into SCE Q9 coefficients.

sources.title: Partisan Trust in the Federal Reserve
sources.access_level: NBER abstract and summary plus the paper's opening sections reviewed; not a complete full-text read.

evidence_locations.claim: Michigan and Gallup data from 2001–2023 show partisan gaps in Fed trust; those gaps do not explain the large partisan gap in inflation expectations. A 2025 survey found Republicans' trust remained lower while their inflation expectations were also lower.
The authors examine same-survey measures of party, Fed trust and inflation expectations and report only a small explanatory role for trust in partisan expectation differences.

findings: Direct counterevidence to a one-direction rule that low institutional trust necessarily means higher inflation expectations.
Open-ended answers point to salient political and tariff information as alternative context for expectation formation.
limitations: The 2025 setting is unusually politicized and the NBER paper is a working paper.
Partisan trust gaps do not identify the effect of general trust on a randomly assigned household.
sources.project_use: Keep trust, partisan information and source use separate; do not code a deterministic trust-to-inflation sign.

sources.title: Information and Macroeconomic Expectations: Global Evidence
sources.access_level: NBER working-paper abstract and metadata read; full paper not read in this pass.

evidence_locations.claim: A harmonized survey of about 47,000 consumers in 47 countries finds local information sources common and associated with biased macroeconomic expectations; distrust in governments and central banks is associated with local-source reliance and less learning from aggregate outcomes.

findings: Information-source selection and institutional trust are relevant to inflation-expectation errors across many countries.
Demographic differences in biases appear largely related to sorting into information sources, rather than different processing of the same information.
limitations: The source-choice and trust relationships are observational; they do not identify the causal effect of assigning a source or changing trust.
The paper's full methods and subgroup definitions were not examined in this pass; the 2023 global sample is not the U.S. SCE.
sources.project_use: Motivates recording information source and source credibility as separate candidate mechanisms; do not infer a respondent's source use from demographics alone.

sources.title: Beliefs About the Economy Are Excessively Sensitive to Household-Level Shocks: Evidence from Linked Survey and Administrative Data
sources.access_level: Full article HTML read in selected sections: abstract, introduction, data/sample, main results and supporting survey evidence; not every appendix table reviewed.

evidence_locations.claim: Danish Consumer Expectations Survey linked to registry data; 35,050 usable responses from 2012–2019 after sample restrictions. Household income changes and expected future household finances covary with inflation forecasts far more than with realized inflation.

Backcasts, adverse health events and supplementary randomized survey prompts support affect-cued recall: negative/positive household events can cue corresponding memories, affecting inflation perceptions and forecasts.

findings: The strongest direct psychological evidence here concerns affect attached to recent or anticipated household events and which inflation memories they cue, rather than a stable optimism trait.
The authors formally test implications of rational expectations and find the observed household-event associations too large to satisfy the benchmark under stated assumptions.
limitations: Administrative income changes are observed, not randomly assigned; the mechanism is described as at least partly affect-cued recall.
The supporting cue experiment does not establish a stable-happiness treatment effect on SCE Q9; Danish survey and register access differ from U.S. public data.
sources.project_use: Prioritize recent/expected household-finance state and salient events as testable candidates; avoid equating them with a general happiness or pessimism score.

sources.title: Fear of the Dark: Inflation Experiences and Subjective Well-being
sources.access_level: Publisher abstract and introduction/data snippets read; full article not read.

evidence_locations.claim: HFCS microdata from 22 countries around 2017 linked to lifetime experienced inflation; higher experience is associated with lower current life-satisfaction scores, with a non-linear pattern in older EU member states.

findings: The direct relationship studied runs from inflation experience to well-being, not from happiness to inflation expectations.
limitations: The result is observational, European and concerns life satisfaction as an outcome; it cannot establish that satisfaction predicts an American household's inflation belief.
sources.project_use: Use as a direction-of-causality caution. Do not cite general inflation-versus-well-being findings as evidence for a happiness persona variable.

sources.title: Subjective Models of the Macroeconomy: Evidence From Experts and Representative Samples
sources.access_level: Publisher abstract and detailed result sections reviewed; full methods and all appendices not read in this pass.

evidence_locations.claim: About 6,500 U.S. households and 1,500 experts forecast inflation and unemployment under common shock vignettes; both groups show within-group disagreement, while households and experts retrieve different demand/supply channels.

findings: Experts' reasoning is more concentrated in textbook channels; household beliefs are dispersed and context-sensitive even under similar stated information.
Context cues can change which causal channel comes to mind and shift forecasts.
limitations: The hypothetical shock vignettes are not ordinary SCE one-year questions or Q9 probability densities.
It does not show that happiness or optimism explains the household–expert gap, nor diagnose this project's model.
sources.project_use: Treat analyst-like reasoning as a testable response-framing hypothesis; compare resident and analyst framing with identical P/E before adding new psychological attributes.
